activity.title: Most Robots built to serve people still feel like black boxes. We wanted to change that. I had one big question coming in as Co-Director of Tech and PM for project Glyph: how can you make a robot more readable to the people it actually interacts with? Our answer: run fluid simulations on the black box. Glyph is a drink-dispensing robot dog equipped with an IMU + LED matrix running real-time fluid dynamics to make the interaction feel more natural. Users can see “liquid” sloshing around as the robot moves and the fluid level decreases as more drinks are dispensed. These goals of improving human-robot interaction have shaped what Terra Labs built for demo this semester: - An end-to-end mobile ordering, autonomous navigation, and drink dispensing system with 3 soda flavors through Glyph - A 7DOF robotic arm serving matcha with an electromagnet end-effector - A projection mapping experience acting as the portal between digital art & people through live hand + face tracking Our club didn’t even exist a semester ago. Because of ~20 cracked engineers + designers, more than 100 people popped out to our showcase. So much love to the talented glyph team: Pan Pitpreecha , Shaurya Goel , Iris Liu Ye , Ellie Lin-Stevens , and Sydney Padilla , it's been so amazing being able to support all of you throughout this past semester. Excited to continue as Co-director of Tech and raise the bar even higher for the next demo! More projects and more unique tech incoming. If you’re interested in what we do, check out our insta and feel free to reach out! 🤖

Just a semester ago I was telling people that I didn't like coding at all. I chose my major because I ONLY wanted to work on circuits. But somewhere between balancing design teams and coursework, I somehow found myself integrating ML models into embedded systems and discovering that I love this intersection. This semester, my team and I built a project to predict Reps in Reserve (proximity to muscular failure) based on the velocity of their repetitions. We used an Arduino Nano to collect and filter Acceleration data, calculate velocity -> ran analysis, rep segmentation/detection, and feature extraction in MATLAB -> trained a Random Forest model -> then ended up converting ALL the MATLAB code to Python to turn it into a full backend -> frontend pipeline. Visualizing the real world data coming from raw sensors and pulling genuine insights made something just click. ECE is a GOATED space between hardware and software. It allows us to bring computational insights to the physical world. Huge thank you to my teammates, Ryan Kim , Akshay Vadlamani , Evan Torrence , Daniel Kim, and Colin Dermyer for grinding through the late nights and into the early mornings, doing everything from tons of Lat pulldowns to last-minute backend redesigns. And thank you to Professor Khan for introducing us to so many facets of ECE then giving the opportunities to apply it in our own ways. Going forward, We're planning to continue improving everything about our project, refining our data collection, models, UI, and expanding our system to encompass a wider range of exercise analytics at a low cost. Here are some of our demos, and we're excited to keep building! Presentation demo: https://lnkd.in/djX9fZ4W Full Tech demo: https://lnkd.in/d9gpu7x9

Over the past few months, I’ve had the privilege of working alongside and learning from some incredible people at Motorola Solutions through my role as a software engineering intern. As a member of Team Theia, I had the opportunity to port a critical diagnostic tool from Python to Golang, reducing its original runtime of 40-45 seconds to under 20 seconds and memory usage from 450-500 MB to 260-290 MB. The enhanced tool will soon be deployed across 70,000 ACUs (Access Control Units), which act as the primary control over door access in key environments like schools, healthcare facilities, and military and government sites. I also had the opportunity to contribute to Motorola Solutions’ cybersecurity initiative, gaining valuable insight into how a Fortune 500 company approaches and maintains cybersecurity at scale. I’m excited to keep developing my software engineering skillset, and I’m grateful to be continuing my work with Motorola Solutions this fall through the co-op program. #solvingforsafer 💙

Watching every one of these interns present their work to Amazon senior leaders and Ring founder Jamie Siminoff was a full-circle moment. These interns tackled real business problems using AI, built real solutions, and shared them with people who know what it takes to build from the ground up. Engineering leaders like Jason Mitura and Iurii G. , managers, and mentors invested countless hours mentoring, challenging, and supporting the interns every step of the way. This summer, I’ve had the chance to see a few very different sides of what it means to build with AI and emerging technology. One of those experiences was PwC ’s inaugural Engineer Your Career program in Seattle. Over four days, I learned from PwC engineers and leaders, visited Microsoft’s campus, and worked with a team through a fast paced immersion challenge based on a real world corporate crisis. Our scenario involved a large scale game developer facing growing customer frustration during a major campaign. Its automated support system could resolve simple tickets, but the company still struggled to respond quickly when issues became more complex and crossed multiple teams. Our team designed a system that gave operations teams direct visibility into the campaign and routed each issue to the right owner. Building the tech was only part of it. The harder part was figuring out how it would actually be introduced, whether teams would adopt it, and whether it could hold up as the company scaled. A tool can be technically impressive and still fail if it doesn’t fit the people, systems, and workflows it has to live within. A huge thank you to PwC for bringing together engineers, students, and builders from across the country, each with a different lens on the same messy problem, and giving us the chance to work through these challenges firsthand. Thank you as well to Fayez Ahmed and Ivan Vinogradov for leading our team and sharing so much about their work and experiences. Novel perspectives, and the chance to keep learning from other builders, is a big part of why I’m extremely excited to attend YC Startup School this week! At Engineer Your Career, I got to see what it takes to apply new technology inside large, complex organizations. At Startup School, I’m excited to explore the other side of that process: how builders identify the right problems, work through uncertainty, and turn early ideas into products and systems that people adopt. If you’ll be at Startup School or around SF this week, let’s meet up!

For the past several months I've been building something I wanted for myself: a place to learn robotics, meet other people building in the space, and share what I'm learning along the way - a real community of learners and roboticists. It's called Leet Robotics, and it's live today. The idea is simple. Courses and learning content, completely free. And alongside them, a cloud workspace - ROS2, simulation, visualization, all pre-installed - so you can actually build, not just read about building. Our first course, Intro to ROS2, is live now: build your first node to a capstone project where a robot autonomously navigates a simulated museum. This is for the students who can't afford a robot. The career switchers who can't justify a full grad program to test if they even like the field. The hobbyists who just want to build something that moves. If that's you, or you know someone it's for, I'd love for you to take a look - and tell me what's missing. https://lnkd.in/gukaxMZK
